utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session. Mr. Registrar, will you call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic and others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 26th of October, 2006, I bid welcome to all those present. I bid good morning to Mr. Mundis, who has rejoined us, the attorneys, and the accused. We begin with the hearing of a witness, but before that two small problems to deal with. I wish to ask the Defence whether in connection with Witness BU there are any requests for the admission of documents. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yesterday afternoon I asked my staff to check the list, and I think we had one, but it is not yet done. It will be done during this morning. So if I may get leave to submit that tomorrow or the day after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Fine. So we'll delay that until tomorrow. Regarding the document when Mr. Praljak -- the one Mr. Praljak showed to the witness regarding the population of the witness's village, my understanding is that Mr. Praljak wants this document to be admitted. After that, we didn't discuss it. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is one of the documents that we will also be submitting together probably tomorrow or on Monday at the latest. My team has been scanning these documents, and that is what we have agreed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just a small remark regarding this document. Yesterday upon reading the document, we found that in that village there was a significant number of Croats, whereas the witness told us in her written statement, but also confirming it orally, that there were only two Croat households in the village. Unfortunately, because we didn't have time, we didn't put the question to the witness for her to explain why there were two households when, in fact, there were dozens of Croats living there during the census. This document is being tendered, but in fact no one put any questions regarding this disparity between the statement of the witness and the fact that there was quite a large number of Croat inhabitants. There must be an explanation. Perhaps the Croats fled. There may be any number of reasons. Perhaps the Defence will come back to that question with other witnesses, but I still wish to draw your attention to this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the sake of information, since you raised this question, the census was from 1981. After that, there was a 1991 census which we will check and use with other witnesses. However, in the case of the 1991 census, there's a formal problem, because we feel that according to the law in force at the time, the 1991 census was not fully completed in accordance with the law. There was no final verification of the results, but the data are probably more or less accurate, and certainly with one of the following witnesses, we will discuss it. Also, I don't think that yesterday's witness could be a person with any significant knowledge of the village's history, so I don't think it would be very useful to discuss the matter with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, good morning. If I may recall, this witness was new in the village, but she said that that was the situation when she came to the village, but she doesn't exclude the possibility of there being more Croats before she came and that they had left. So she was talking only about the actual situation in the village at the time she was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is true. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Mr. President, although the witness clearly wasn't asked directly about the census numbers and the relationship between her earlier testimony, I would call to the Chamber's attention the line of questioning reflected in yesterday's transcript at pages 45 and 46 wherein Judge Trechsel did ask her some questions concerning the numbers of Croat families that left, and it would seem to be from her testimony that at the time of the war there were only two Croat families left and that others had left prior to that point in time. But again, I draw your attention to pages 45 and 46. It's clear that those questions were not put to her in the context of the documents specifically, but she does in response to Judge Trechsel, she did discuss that, that point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Judges will closely deliberate on this matter. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. A totally different matter, Your Honour. As you might well know, I'm sure you all know, under Rule 65 there are possibilities to have meetings outside a courtroom setting, and I would urge the Trial Chamber to consider, perhaps, setting up a 65 ter meeting simply because I think it might be a way for us to deal with housekeeping matters, perhaps have a frank exchange of ideas that have not -- without taking the courtroom time. I know that in -- in other cases, in my previous case we availed ourselves to those situations whenever we had a technical issue and didn't have the time. Usually it's -- outside the presence of the accused, but a record could be made, but nonetheless, I think it's a good opportunity to have an exchange of ideas, because I must say I'm -- I'm at the point where I find that there may be some differences of opinions. I certainly don't want to give the impression that I'm disrespectful to the Trial Chamber. Perhaps there are other issues as well that we could resolve, and I certainly think that we could find ways to be much more efficient in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas, for your suggestion. We will discuss it already this afternoon, and we will let you know what is our view. Mr. Mundis, do you have any comments on the part of the Prosecution regarding the suggestion by Mr. Karnavas? Do you support it, oppose it? Are you neutral?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the prospect of a 65 ter meeting with the Chamber's legal officers or -- would certainly be something that the Prosecution would be amenable to doing at any point in time during the course of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding of what Mr. Karnavas said was that it would be a 65 ter meeting, Defence counsel, Judges, and the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask Your Honours to allow me to address two points. The first is that two days ago, we received a ruling of the court on the non-admission of certain documents regarding the Mujahedin and the number of Croats killed in various ways in 21 municipalities which I prepared. The explanation is that a crime does not justify another crime, and I'm sure that no one in his right mind would claim such a thing, but the justification of one crime by another and explanations of crimes are quite a different matter. So I'd like Your Honours to let me know, either orally or in writing, how I can explain this. The second point regards the Mujahedin. This directly affects the indictment, which says that Mujahedin did not represent anything more than a means for the Croats to frighten other Croats with the threat of Mujahedins. I think the situation is quite different in the method of their warfare, the numbers in which they came, the transformation of the war into a religious war, and that is why I would like to have the opportunity to explain why the Mujahedin were very important, especially with respect to the conflict between the Croat and Muslim people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Yesterday, we heard the word used -- words to the effect that Croats attacked, Croats expelled, et cetera. These were either units out of control or under some control. We spent half a century living in a society with collective responsibility. The Croats were Ustashas, the Serbs were Chetniks, and since this Court was an institution formed to -- reconciliation, I think we should never use a collective noun as the perpetrators. It's not that the Croats that expelled the Bosniaks or the Bosniaks the Croats, but this was done by individuals, and according to my statistics, about 90 per cent of these perpetrators had names and surnames. So we can individualise the guilt. And by saying in such a public trial that the Croats killed the Bosniaks and the Bosniaks killed the Croats I think is not appropriate, because using such collective nouns implies collective responsibility which does not exist in law, especially as those Croats admitted half a million refugees. We're trying to individualise guilt. We have to know who is guilty for each crime. So I think the use of such collective nouns should be avoided at all cost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Praljak, regarding the question that you have raised, we have replied in a rendered decision personally, and I speak only in my own name. I wish to tell you that defence tu quoque is not admitted in this Trial Chamber. This tu quoque has absolutely no value, because according to humanitarian law, this type of defence is excluded. Regarding the other question of the Mujahedin, there will be witnesses who are going to come, and you will have the possibility of re-introducing your documents, because the witness through whom you wanted to have those documents admitted was not one capable of authenticating the documents. So I think you will have the opportunity as soon as next week to re-introduce this again. So the rejection was based on points of law and opportunities with this witness, so you will have other occasions to re-introduce this. We have taken note of everything that you have said, and you must know that the Judges bear all these elements in mind. It is now a quarter past 9.00. We are going to bring in the witness. Shall we bring down the blinds, because there is a request of protective measures, and we need to deal with that probable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. The Defence of Mr. Petkovic would like to address one or two of the principles in relation to protective measures in open session, taking great care, as of course we would, to ensure that nothing is said in an open session which could preempt any decision and could lead to any identification of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give you the floor, but after we have brought in the witness. And also, we have to pull down the blinds so that the witness cannot be seen by the audience. You will have the floor in a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's understood, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to private session now, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that we're in open session, madam, could you tell me your first and last names and your date of birth again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zijada Kurbegovic, the 25th of January, 1965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, do you have a profession? Are you employed or are you a housewife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm employed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work in Gornji Vakuf, in a pharmacist's shop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, have you already testified before a national or International Tribunal with regard to the events that took place in your country in the 1990s, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll put a question to you that I have never put to a witness so far, however, I have to do this now. You were interviewed by an investigator from the Office of the Prosecution. Can you confirm the fact that you did meet with an investigator from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm referring to an investigator from the OTP who went to your country to interview you, after which you signed a written statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you also interviewed -- or have you also been interviewed by an investigator in your own country, from your own country, with regard to the events you were a witness of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the war, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, after the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was only on that occasion that I gave that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please, could you read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please sit down. I'd like to provide you with some information about the procedure we will be following during this hearing. You will first have to answer the questions put to you by Mr. Mundis, whom you have already met. According to what I have been told, Mr. Mundis will be needing an hour and a half, but perhaps he will need less time. Once this stage has been completed, the Defence, who are to your left, will put their questions to you within the framework of what we call the cross-examination. They will have about an hour and a half, and that means each Defence team will have 15 minutes. The Judges will make sure they don't use up any additional time. The four Judges sitting before you may also put questions to you at any point in time. You will notice that when Judges put questions to you, the nature of their questions is quite different from those put to you by the other parties. The questions Judges put to you are put to you in order to confirm or clarify certain answers that you provide to the Prosecution and to the Defence. We also put questions to witnesses to verify what you have said in relation to the indictment. We have to verify certain facts in this way. If there are any questions that you fail to understand, don't hesitate to ask the party putting the question to you to rephrase it or to put it to you again. We'll be having 20-minute breaks every one and a half hours. This should allow you to rest. The next break will at about 10.30. Before I give the floor to Mr. Mundis, Mr. Mundis, last week I told the Prosecution that when proofing witnesses, if it seems that a witness might have health problems of any kind, you should inform the Chamber of the fact. I have just found out from the registrar that this witness might have a certain condition. I'm not sure whether you are aware of the fact or not. If so, just say so and we won't go into the details. Otherwise, we will have to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we were also just informed by the Registry via e-mail of that. I'm not sure if the investigator who assisted me yesterday with proofing had asked that question during the preliminary meeting. So I will ensure that our practices reflect what the Trial Chamber has requested us to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll now ask the registrar to move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally, I would like to ask the Defence to take this fact into consideration. I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Ma'am, can you please tell us where you were living in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I was living in the village of Uzricje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And with whom were you living?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I was living with my husband, my two children, and my mother-in-law, father-in-law, two relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the ethnic composition of Uzricje in early 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There were Muslims and Croats. The population was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give us an estimate about the percentages of those two groups living in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you any percentages. There were perhaps about 400 inhabitants. The Muslims were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the relations between the Muslims and Croats in Uzricje in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The relations were normal. There were no problems of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you describe a little bit about the beginning of the war in Bosnia? When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the actual war broke out on the 13th of January, but prior to that date, in November, 1992, there had been brief skirmishes, attacks on the village. But on the 13th of January, 1993, there was a full-blown war that broke out in Uzricje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's me ask you actually, Witness, if we could back up a little bit. In the summer of 1992, to your knowledge, did the war start in Bosnia in the wider context of the entire country?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the war with the Serbs started, but in Uzricje the population grew a bit. Refugees arrived from Donji Vakuf, from Modrica. They'd fled before the Serbian aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how far from Uzricje was the war with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's about 32 kilometres from Gornji Vakuf to Donji Vakuf, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was the front line between the Serbs and the combined Muslim and Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the front line was down in the direction of Donji Vakuf and Mackovac and Radusa were the lines further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the men in the village of Uzricje when the war started with the Serbs? What did the men do?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Croats and Muslims worked together but then they started digging dugouts so that they could have some sort of security, so they could have shelters. They went to these jointly held lines. They went there together. But in November -- as of November and up until the 13th of January, everything changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start, Witness, with November. You're talking about November 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in November -- in early November, 1992, what were the relations like between the Muslims and the Croats in Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They were quite normal until an attack was launched on the village. And after the attack, they no longer held these joint lines, but there were no disputes among us neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about this attack that you've told us about that was launched on the village in November, 1992? Do you recall the specifics of that incident?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it didn't last for long, several hours. We were in the village, so we heard that shooting, and it didn't last for long as I said, only a few hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After this first incident, this first attack in November, 1992, how did the situation in the village change?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Mundis. Allow me to intervene at this point. It's necessary to be very precise. Given the witness's answer, I'm somewhat confused. Madam, you mentioned an attack in November. As a general rule, when an attack is launched, you have one party who is the first party to open fire and then someone responds. When you say there was an attack, who first opened fire according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Croats started the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how do you know this? On what basis do you claim that the Croats started? Because it could be a member of the Territorial Defence or of the ABiH who opens fire or who opened fire, and then the other side reacts. On what basis do you claim that the Croats started opening fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I heard. I said that I wasn't there, that I wasn't in town. I said that immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this is something that you were told.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me further clarify. This -- this attack that you've just told us about in November, 1992, was this attack in the village of Uzricje or was it in somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was just in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say in the town, what town are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How far is the town of Gornji Vakuf from Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So just so we're absolutely clear, when this attack was launched where were you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were in Uzricje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell it us how the situation in Uzricje changed following this attack on Gornji Vakuf in November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation changed after that event. We heard shelling between Gornji Vakuf and Uzricje. We heard the sound of shelling. We were in the middle of the village, all together. Croats and Muslims were there. Then we were told that these shells were being fired from Idovac by the Serbs, but that wasn't clear. They were taking coordinates from Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You say you were told the shells were being fired from Idovac by the Serbs. Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were there and Croats were telling us how the Serbs were shelling from up there and that's what we thought too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After this attack in November, 1992, were any steps taken to defend the village of Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were the Croats and Muslims who were together again. I'm not sure whether there was a checkpoint there. I wasn't at the site, but the Croats and Muslims were together. But Muslim women and our husbands didn't go anywhere, whereas they, two or three days earlier, on the 13th, had left the village. The Croatian women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that incident or that event in just a moment, but let me again focus your attention on November, 1992. After this first attack, were there any subsequent attacks before January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was another attack launched by the Croats. This was obvious because they only opened fire on the part of the town that is called Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Witness, when you refer to the town, which town are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: To Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At what point in time, to the best of your recollection, did this second attack on Mahala take place?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I am afraid I can't remember quite exactly, but it was maybe 10, 15, 20 days before the attack on the 13th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following or during the time, roughly, when this attack on Mahala took place, what steps were taken, if any, in the village of Uzricje to defend the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing was done. I told you a moment ago we were together to prevent people entering the village thinking that the Serbs might come in. We were together. We couldn't assume that it could be the Croats. We were allies in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During this time period from November, 1992, until January, 1993, were there any fortifications or trenches or anything like that built in the village of Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Two dugouts. Two dugouts were prepared again together. Croats and Muslims dug them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where were these two dugouts?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: One was about -- near the centre of the village, and the other was in the lower part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the size of these dugouts and how they were actually constructed?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The upper dugout that I went to, that I was in, was roughly, roughly 3 by 4 metres, roughly. It was dug into a hillside, and inside it was lined with planks, wooden planks. It was covered by nylon. And in inside there were no facilities, but it was a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean by it was covered by nylon?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: It was wintertime and there was a lot of humidity, and we had to protect ourselves from the precipitation. So this was a plastic cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the dugout have a door or doors?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There was just one door to enter the dugout, made from wooden boards to keep the cold out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say there were no facilities, was there any electricity in the dugout?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. No electricity, no water. It's just a hole in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was the second dugout?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The other dugout was in the lower part of the village. I didn't enter it, but I assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, madam. We are hearing the French translation "casemate", in English, "dugout". This dugout, was it a bunker? Was it constructed in hard material, in cement, or as you are saying, a hole in the ground? Were the walls made of concrete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It was precisely a hole in the ground but just lined with wooden boards and protected with plastic sheeting to avoid water entering it. So this was just an emergency shelter that we could hide in and seek protection in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This hole in the ground, what security did it provide in relation to a cave? Was it any better than a cave? This could also be a hole in the ground. In what sense did this hole provide greater security for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It gave us greater security because these villages have underground waters and our houses don't have cellars. This was about 50 metres away from our houses, and there was this small hillock, and this dugout was dug into the hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this clarification, because according to my understanding, I had imagined it was more of a bunker, but this is more like a shelter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, a few moments ago you mentioned this attack of the 13th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. I think it is not opportune to talk about an attack. My learned friend keeps referring to an attack, and we don't really know what was happening there, nor did the witness explicitly mention attack. I think it is better to refer to an incident until we actually establish what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure Mr. Mundis is going to specify. If not, I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. Page 26, line 14, the witness answered: "I'm afraid I can't remember quite exactly, but it was maybe 10, 15, 20 days before the attack on the 13th of January." The witness has referred to this incident as an attack. I'm simply using the language that the witness herself used in characterising this incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, did anything unusual happen in the village of Uzricje a few days before this incident or attack on the 13th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were together, and two or three days before this event the Croatian women left the village, but in our village, a lady had a chicken farm, so both Croatian and Muslim women went to purchase from her, and an elderly Croat lady said, "If Ruza," that was her name, "leaves," that is the Croat lady whose name was Ruza, "If she leaves the village, it's over." However, that is what actually happen. Ruza also left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you come to know that the Croatian women left the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This man, this Muslim who was with a Croat, he told us, because they were together, this some sort of a check-point. I wasn't there, so I don't know what it looks like. He was there when all the Croatian women abandoned the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the Croatian men?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you just mentioned a check-point. Where was this check-point in the village, and was it held by a Croats and a Muslim together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was at the exit of the village when you leave Uzricje to go to Mackovac. And, yes, there was a Croat and a Muslim there together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Muslim, he was a member of the Territorial Defence or the BH army, or was he a civilian who was in the company of the Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were all civilians in those days, but I think it was the Territorial Defence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, at the time when the Croatian women left the village, where were the Croatian men?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They stayed in the village. I didn't see them, but that's what this man said, that they remained in the village. They didn't leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what about the Bosniak men? In early to mid-January, 1993, what were they doing in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They were there. Everybody went about his own business. No one didn't go anywhere except for those who jointly performed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, in answer to the Prosecution, you said that the women left the village and that the men stayed behind, the Croat men. This may appear to be a strange event, because when a woman leaves her husband, this can be either because of family differences or some important reason. But when the women left the village, what was being said in the village? What was the reason that had prompted the women to leave? And I also assume that they took the children with them. I can't imagine the women going without the children. So what was the reason for these Croatian women to leave the village as far as you were able to gather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that both the women and children had left, Croatian women and children. The men stayed behind. It was said that an attack was being expected from Idovac by the Serbs, that there would be heavy shelling. That is what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Was there any talk about the Muslim women and children also leaving? It is a bit change that if the Serbs threatened to attack, only one group of the village leaves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't go anywhere, because we didn't believe that any such thing could happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you didn't believe that the Serbs were going to shell the village, and that is why you stayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that, that we didn't believe that they would shell, but they just thought there would be a shell just like any other shell, and we'd be in the dugout and it would blow over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, on page 31, lines 7 and 8, you answered, "It was said that an attack was being expected. That is what they said." Who told you that an attack was to be expected from the Serbs at Idovac?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Croats told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Mundis. We are touching upon crucial issues. Idovac, how far is it from your village, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I can't tell you exactly. It's a mountainous area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But roughly, 5 kilometres, 10 kilometres, 1 kilometre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something like that. Let's say 10 kilometres, roughly, but I can't tell you with precision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you about the distance in order to see whether, according to you, even though you're not a specialist in artillery matters, was it possible to fire a shell at your village from a distance of several kilometres? What is your answer, because it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At this time point in early to mid-January, 1993, when the Croatian women and children left the village, what were the Bosniak men doing?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing. They were just there doing their regular work. They -- they were just there, and nobody went anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, if --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think we have a problem with the record, because the witness said they distributed themselves there. I'd like to ask her what exactly she meant. They -- that's exactly what the witness said, so I'd like our learned friend to check this with the witness, what she meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please specify, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, did you say that the people had distributed themselves and, if so, who distributed themselves and where?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: There, when they were there, they spread out there, Croats and Muslims. They were together; one Croat, one Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were they in any way attempting to defend the village together, the Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. When the attack started, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you. Before -- immediately before the attack, when you say they were spread out there, Croats and Muslims, they were together, one Croat, one Muslim, what do you mean? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, they were there on this road so as to avoid anyone entering the village. I wasn't there. I didn't see it. I don't know what the road looked like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, listening to you, it has occurred to me to ask: In your village, was there a municipal authority? Was there a mayor, any kind of authority, leader, in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the local board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us there was the local board. So I assume if there is a possibility of an attack by the Serbs which leads to the departure of a part of the population, women and children, would the local board meet to discuss the matter, which after all is serious? So as far as you know, was there a meeting of the local board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there was a meeting, but it was discussed in the village jointly. That was the main subject. The men of the village, both Croats and Muslims, would be debating the issue and discussing it, but the women were not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, in your village when a problem occurs, who deals with it? By the inhabitants themselves, or by the local authority or by the military? Who deals -- or who dealt with problems in the village at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was the locals, the villagers. They would resolve everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you tell us -- I'd now like focus your attention on the 13th of January, 1993. What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, I think it was in the afternoon of the 13th of January, the shells started falling. There was heavy shelling. We didn't have time for anything. We rushed immediately into the dugout. Myself and my family and the whole neighbourhood, some went to the lower dugout, depending on which was closer. And from then on, from the 13th of January on, we spent nine days and nine nights in this dugout.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the nine days and nine nights that you were in the dugout, did you at any point leave the dugout?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the evening when it gets real dark, we would go out to fetch water and some food that remained in those houses, because during those nine days and houses of -- nine days and nights of shelling, some houses had been damaged, some totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not being very specific. You said that there were nine days of shelling. Was it continuous, there was a shelling falling every five minutes, or was it shelling that was occasional, with interruptions, or did the shells keep falling all the time, which forced you to stay in this hole? Could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The shelling was non-stop, day and night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your language I heard the word "nonstop," so I assume that it is an established term in your language. So it was continuous, uninterrupted shelling. My colleague has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, according to your statement the women and children, that is the Croat women and children, left the village. So I assume in these shelters there were Muslim women and children. But you also said Croat and Muslim men stayed in the village. Were they all also in the shelter during the shelling? I'm talking about Muslim and Croat men. Were they also in the shelters, or were they somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 13th, I don't know what happened to the Croatian men, because I was in this dugout and they were not with me in the dugout. So I can't say because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 12th of January, in the afternoon or evening, the Croatian men, were they still in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they were not in your shelter, there was another shelter. Could they have been in the other shelter, or did they flee during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't claim that. I can't say. I don't know. I didn't see anything with my own eyes, so I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the Bosniak men from Uzricje? Once you had gone into the dugout, where were the Bosniak men?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly the elderly men, the women and children, both older and younger ones, were in the dugout, whereas the men who were -- I don't know how to put it -- who were able to carry a rifle, in their 30s, they were there. Some had Kalashnikovs, some had hunting rifles, and they were just above this dugout, above and around the dugout in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that at night you would leave the dugout to get food and water. When you left the dugout, did you see people in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't see anyone in the village, but when one went from the dugout toward one's houses, from the hills, a hill called Mackovac facing us, we saw there buses. Were they trucks or buses, they had strong headlights, and we could see them coming in our direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And a final couple of question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may just intervene. Madam, you have said that there had been incessant shelling without interruption. Should you perhaps correct this as far as the night is concerned? You said you went out during the night. Was there also a certain pause or a slowing down of the rhythm of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was a slowing down, but when you're going to fetch food for your children, you don't care whether there's shelling or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A follow-up question to that of my colleague. When you left for the first time and the next times, were you able to see that the buildings had been hit by the shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. My house was damaged at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many houses, to the best of your recollection? How many houses were damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I was in the central part of the village and in the upper dugout, this part was heavily damaged. Virtually each and every house was damaged by the end of those nine days and nights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to the best of your knowledge, everyone sought shelter in the two shelters, or did some people remain in their houses and they may have been killed or wounded by the shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, and according to what I saw, the upper part of the village had been abandoned and everyone from that part was in the dugout. No one stayed behind. So everyone went to the dugout that was closest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That would be an appropriate time for the first recess, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is 10.30. We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you tell us approximately how many people were in this 3 by 4 square metre dugout with you during these nine days and nights?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think there were perhaps about 30 of us, perhaps 40, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, at the end of this nine-day period what happened?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the end of this nine-day period spent in the dugout, I don't know whether it was in the morning, I didn't have a watch, I don't know what time it was exactly, but at one point in time a Croatian soldier kicked the door in and opened the door in this way, and he said, "Please don't panic, but leave the dugout." When leaving the dugout -- well, even if it had been my brother, I wouldn't have been able to recognise him because his face had perhaps been painted black. It was completely covered in paint, and on his sleeve he had HVO insignia. And when going down the small hill towards the middle of the village, the soldiers were at a distance of perhaps two, two and a half metres from each other. Some had certain blue ribbons on their sleeves and others had orange ribbons. And we left this upper dugout, the one that I was in, and when we gathered at this point, they said, "Whoever has a weapon should place it aside." But one of the soldiers said, "You should thank God, because yesterday it was very dark. Otherwise, none of you would have survived." And then they placed us in two houses, in the house of Kurbegovic Cazim and in the house of Ibrahim Kurbegovic. They didn't separate the men from the women and children, but they just said that some of us should go to one of the houses and others to the other house. But we were told that the women and children should go to Kurbegovic Ibrahim's home, house, and they would write down our names and surnames. And the men were in front of the Semka Filipovic's house. They were left there. And when the women and children went -- the Muslim women and children arrived in Ibrahim Kurbegovic's house, a man introduced himself to us. He was a soldier and he said that his name was Pile. He said that he had to take down our names so he would know how many of us there were, but he said that he also had five children of his own and that nothing would happen to us while he was there. He said that his children cried as our children did. And after they had compiled this list, everyone went to the house he or she had been assigned to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, let me interrupt you at this point. Approximately how many soldiers did you see in the village when you came out of the dugout?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but when we were in the middle of the village, there was certainly 20 or 30 soldiers who were armed, and I saw others in the house, and they were setting fire to these houses, and they would also fire shots using incendiary bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And which houses did you see being set on fire?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They only set fire to Muslim houses. Not a single Croatian house was damaged. They all remained intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if any Croatian houses were damaged due to shelling?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once you were taken --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just to be absolutely clear. Witness, you said, "No." Does that mean you do not know, or does it mean no houses were damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no damaged houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, a minute ago you said that they opened fire and used incendiary bullets. Did you personally see a soldier open fire at a house as a result of which the house was set on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, the shelling lasted for nine days. At the end of nine days, only Muslim houses had been destroyed, and no Croatian houses had been hit by the shelling. That seems a little strange to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, how do you explain the fact that it's possible to shell a village over a nine-day period and some houses, as if by chance, were not damaged and only Muslim houses were damaged? Can you explain this phenomenon, which might seem to be quite extraordinary? At least it might seem to be extraordinary initially, but I am waiting for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do think it was an extraordinary situation, because there were some houses that were mixed. There were some houses that were among Muslim houses, but not a single one was damaged. I don't know whether that's because they were so professional, but it's quite true to say that not a single one was damaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you're also referring to the shelling that was carried out at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not a single house was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, when you were taken out of the dugout and directed into one of these two houses, was that the part of the village that was mixed, or was that predominantly the Muslim part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the part where they were in the majority. Only one or two houses belonged to Croats. They were next to the house or in the vicinity of the house I was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, because you've mentioned the two houses, which of the two houses were you directed to go to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I was sent to Cazim Kurbegovic's house, which was next to those Croatian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Cazim Kurbegovic's house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I stayed there till we actually left the village of Uzricje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that we left the village of Uzricje in March or April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how many people were in Cazim Kurbegovic's house during this time period?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think there were about 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe the 20 people in terms of their gender, age, ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They were Muslims, and as for their age, there were children, and there were elderly people up to 70 years of age too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there men and women in that house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Men and women. They were all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during the time period that you were there in 1993, early part of 1993, did you remain in that house the entire period or did you go out at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: When necessary, because the person who compiled this list said that since we had livestock, he said that we could go out up until 4.00 in the afternoon to feed the livestock, to carry out these tasks, if we had such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you in fact go out to feed the livestock during this time period?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Only on one occasion with my mother-in-law. I couldn't do that more frequently.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: With my father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And on this one occasion when you went to feed the livestock with your father-in-law, what, if anything, did you observe in the village of Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they continued to set fire to buildings. If everything hadn't been destroyed, they would blow-up buildings. When we set off from the small hill near our village and went down the road, someone would see you and they'd shout out to us, "Put your hands behind your backs and walk down the middle of the road." So someone was protecting us there from -- from the Croatian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you some follow-on questions from what you've just told us. You said they continued to set fire to buildings. On this occasion when you went out of the house with your father-in-law, did you actually see any buildings on fire personally?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I saw the house because I was staying in Cazim Kurbegovic's house, and across the road from his house there was Subka Hozic's house. I saw her house being set on fire. She had chickens in front of the house. They killed all her chickens. They asked my father-in-law whether he had a match there in order to set fire to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who -- who -- when you say, "They killed all her chickens," who is the "they" that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The Croats, because they still had the insignia on their sleeves. The same insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what insignia was that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: HVO insignia. And sometimes they had blue ribbons on them or orange ribbons, but I couldn't see their faces clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You also mentioned a few moments ago they would blow-up buildings. Do you recall hearing anything that sounded like an explosion?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you have just mentioned these people with the HVO insignia who also had ribbons on them. As you have said that you spend a number of weeks in the village, you stayed there for a number of weeks, did these HVO members -- or were these HVO members the same throughout this period, or did you see any new individuals? And those who remained there, did they always have their faces painted black?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I went out, they always had their faces painted. Later, I couldn't go out, but there was one person who came there and asked to go to the toilet. He entered. He said that he had come from Australia. And I only saw his face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Madam, for the second time now, you have said that you could not -- you were not able to go out. Could you explain why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because I was afraid. I was afraid to go out. I didn't dare go out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you wanted to go out, would someone have opened fire on you? Would one have prevented you from going out or leaving the village even?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No one left the village, but my father-in-law naturally went to feed the livestock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A while ago you mentioned this individual who went to use the toilet in the house, and he told you that he had come from Australia. I assume that he spoke to you in your own language, or did he speak to you in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He spoke to me in our language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was it possible for you to identify him on the basis of his accent? Could you tell which part of your country he was from, or were you unable to detect a particular accent of any kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He spoke normally. I couldn't really say now how he spoke, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, during the time period that you were in Cazim Kurbegovic's house, to your knowledge, did anyone leave the village? Any of the Bosniaks, that is, leave the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the conditions like in this -- in that house while you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we had water, only water. We didn't have any electricity. We had stoves that we could use for heating. We used the food that had remained in those two houses. That's what we had. There were two rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time period that you were in Cazim Kurbegovic's house, was anyone wounded or did anyone die?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. While we were there, a van arrived in front of our house, the house that I was staying in, and it took Kurbegovic Azim and Seketa Sukrija away. They were driven to Prozor. And on that occasion, Camka Seketa died because she was seriously ill. She was an old woman, an exhausted woman. She died during that period of time and then there was Avdo Seketa and Mehmed Seketa, but later, Sulejman Filipovic, after he had been taken away in the village somewhere, they beat him up and he died soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who took him away or who beat him up?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see this, but in the morning his sons -- his son's wife, his daughter-in-law, came and said, "Help me. They've killed my father-in-law." They don't know who took him away. They had some sort of caps on their heads. I don't know if they could recognise them on the basis of their voices, but he was beaten up badly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, let's be precise again. You said that there was an elderly woman who died. What I would like to know is whether she died in the house, and did you actually see her dead body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She didn't die there. In fact, she was there. A Croatian neighbour of ours took her to their part of town, to the Croatian part. I don't know whether they took her to see the doctor, but she died in a Croatian house, and she was buried in Uzricje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How old was she, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think she was between 70 and 75 years old for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned Filipovic who was beaten up and died, but you personally saw nothing. This is something that you were told by Filipovic's daughter-in-law.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I neglected to ask you earlier. On the 13th of January, 1993 -- let me rephrase that. When you came out of the dugout approximately nine days after the 13th of January, 1993, were any of the Bosniaks from the village killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two persons were killed, Jusuf Softic, also known as Softa, and Tahir Plivcic, who was a refugee from Donji Vakuf. They were killed on that day, on the very same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened to these two individuals?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we were taken out of the dugout and when we arrived in the centre of the village, they asked Softic Jusuf where his house was, where he lived. He pointed to his house. He said, "That's my house." Tahir Plivcic was next to him. They asked him, "Where do you live?" He said, "I'm a refugee, and I'm staying in his house." They said, "Come here." They set off in the direction of that house. We went down to the house we'd been assigned to. That's the last time I saw them. But when Pile compiled this list of us in Ibrahim's house, Ibro told us that those two men had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you tell us about the situation when you left Uzricje? Can you tell us approximately when that was and where you went to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time I think it was March or April, as I said a while ago, and there was some sort of a truce, but a van arrive. And during this truce, we tried to clean up our households. My husband and children went to clean up our house. A van with five soldiers arrived, and they told him that they had to go and see those people who had stayed in Uzricje and to inform them that we had to leave Uzricje. So we had to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: And that's when we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me just ask you if you can tell us, this van with the five soldiers, what military force were these soldiers from who came in this van?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They were from the Croatian army, because they told my husband, "We can't be like you," they said, "Like you Muslims. You captured our two soldiers. That is why you must leave the village now."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say Croatian army, are you sure it was the Croatian army, or was it the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see any -- did you see any insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't because I was on a balcony. I was on a balcony. I just saw camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you told us a few moments ago, "That's when we left," can you tell us how you left and where you went?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I went with my children to the area known as the Mahala, which was a purely Muslim area. We went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where -- where is Mahala?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Mahala is in Gornji Vakuf, the upper part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you get from Uzricje to Mahala?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We went along the main road, and no one hurt us or bothered us. We passed through the Croatian part of the town and reached the Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you walk or were you in a vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, can you tell us -- you've mentioned several times about houses being damaged or destroyed or burned. Can you tell us approximately how many houses in the village of Uzricje were damaged or destroyed or burned?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think -- as this is a small village, I think some 30 or 40 households were destroyed at the time. And that implies houses and stables and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask now that the witness be shown a video which is P 1027. We would ask that this be played without the audio, just the video. I would also inform everyone that there's a lengthy segment in the middle of this video where an individual is speaking. We have removed most of that with the exception of a brief clip showing this individual. I'm going to ask the witness if she can identify anything on the videotape. It runs less than 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And after that you will be finished, because I have looked at the clock, and I'm counting on the Defence having an hour and a half, and we should normally adjourn at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I -- just after this video, Mr. President, I have one more document to show this witness and that would be the completion of the direct examination. I think I've used about 45 minutes today based on our calculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, we're going to show you this videotape. I would ask you -- and I should also inform everyone the quality of this videotape is not very good. Witness, I would ask you, as we did yesterday, if you see anything on the tape that you recognise, persons or places or houses, to simply say stop as soon as you see it, and we will do our best to pause it so that you can identify whatever it is on the tape that you recognise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who this person is?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is Ibrahim Kurbegovic, who is from Uzricje, and a part of the population was in his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what the building is behind Ibrahim Kurbegovic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a stable. I think it's a stable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. This is at the end of the village. We called this Harman, where children played basketball, and this is Hozic Omer's house and that of his son.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I think that's actually the end of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, to the best of your knowledge, what's depicted on this videotape?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment, Mr. Mundis. Before asking the witness this question, can you tell us where this video comes from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It comes from the Bosnian AID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What's that AID of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's the Agency for Information and Documentation. It's an investigative agency of the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask Mr. Mundis whether we received this material among the Prosecution documents, and I think we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you disclose to the accused and the Defence a copy of this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My case manager assures me, Mr. President and Your Honours, that as this was an exhibit and has been on our exhibit list that it would have been disclosed to the Defence some time ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED CORIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I ask this because I wanted to be sure whether I saw this, and I did, and I remember well talking to this person who is answering a question where the reserve positions of the soldiers are. And I now hear this silent film and another version with a lot of material which would be of great significance for what we're talking about. So I don't know why the tone was switched off. I really don't understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I would like to support the remark of Mr. Coric. Why did you decide to eliminate the sound? And also, this video that we looked at for a few minutes must be a part of other scenes, and Mr. Coric tells us that the person we see was answering a question put by somebody regarding his membership of the reserve force or something like that. What can you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was partially in order to save time. On the actual videotape itself, there is approximately three minutes of Mr. Kurbegovic speaking to someone who is off camera, and we simply, as a means of trying to save some time, because that didn't really add anything to this witness's particular testimony, we chose this course of action. Of course, we can play the entire videotape with the audio. Any of the Defence teams can do the same thing if they think it's important and relevant for their cases. We simply made the decision, given the fact that -- that the main purpose was to have the witness identify what's on the videotape and the locations on the videotape and not to have her testify concerning what Ibrahim Kurbegovic said on the videotape. It's simply for that reason and that reason alone. Of course, any of the Defence teams can play that if they think it's important or relevant during -- during the cross-examination or at any point later in the trial for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, to the best of your knowledge, can you tell us where this videotape was taken, what location?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was taken at Uzricje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I have just one more document to show the witness which is P 7350.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Actually, I showed you this document yesterday. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to take a look at this document?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This document identifies a number of individuals who were allegedly involved in looting and torching in Uzricje. Do you know any of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I know Marko Livajsic. He was a neighbour. Marinko Livajsic, also a neighbour. Mato, I don't know. Bero, I don't know. I don't know the others. I know these two because they were from my neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point during the first three months of 1993, that is January through March or into even April, did you see either Marko Livajsic or Marinko Livajsic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you see them?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In Uzricje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, have either of these individuals been brought to trial for looting or burning in Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions. We would tender the videotape and P 7350.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, just a question on the basis of the document. At the very end of the document it says that Croats evicted -- hated the Muslims of the village, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, they aided the Muslims. Correction. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you confirm that indeed two Croats in this village did help you, did help the Muslims of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There as also a list of soldiers. You said Marko Livajsic, that you know him. You know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because in this document, it is indicated that he was the HVO commander in your village. What do you think of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I can't say, because I wasn't involved in that. So I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question on the basis of this document, dated the 27th of December, 1993, says that about 70 houses whose owners were Muslims were burnt, destroyed, et cetera. Does this figure appear to you to correspond to the truth, the number of destroyed houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a moment ago that I didn't know the exact number of houses, but I think that would be about right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you said that you knew Marko Livajsic, the commander of the HVO in your village. Do you know where he is today? Do you still see him or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is still in Uzricje. He is now in Uzricje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence now, without any further loss of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will leave our time for the other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours. I have no -- no questions for the witness. I just wish, however, to point out, based on the last document, that this is a -- looks like it's an Official Note. There's no documentation that an investigation was conducted that would lead to any criminal trials or prosecutions. So in fairness to the Defence, the Prosecution should have asked perhaps whether an investigation was done. Simply asking whether a trial occurred is insufficient evidence to establish this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have a few questions. I'd like to start with the last document since we still have it before us. My colleague is trying to find it, but I'm sure we'll find it in the course of my cross-examination. We're trying to find a reference to what the witness said about the houses that were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, didn't you say that between 30 and 40 houses in the village had been destroyed, and now when this question was put to you by the Presiding Judge -- yes, we've just found the reference, page 12, lines 12 to 13. When asked by the Presiding Judge, you said that perhaps there were 70 houses that had been destroyed, but here you said between 30 and 40 houses. What is in fact correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
