utterances.text: At the outset, I said that I wasn't sure. I said I didn't know exactly how many houses had been destroyed. I never counted them. And I said that the Muslim houses were most numerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But, madam, you would agree that there is a difference between 30 and 40 houses and 70 houses. 70 is almost as twice as many, so you couldn't have made such a mistake. So what is in fact what you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said about 30 houses, madam. Thirty households. I mentioned stables too. So I said there were some houses and there were some stables.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You didn't say some houses and some stables the first time round, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, perhaps you could assist the Chamber, because in English it says "buildings." In your language, in B/C/S, what does the word mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you looking at the transcript for the document? Which translation are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Building" is the term that appears in the translation. What I would like to know is the term in your own language. Perhaps it's the term "Objekt". Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking the interpreters to tell me whether this term refers to houses or buildings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter note: It refers to buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreters have told me that the word means buildings. It could be a house. It could be a building of another kind. It could be anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do agree with you, but in response to a question put to the witness by the Prosecution with regard to how many buildings had been destroyed, she said between 30 and 40, and this is why I'm now asking her about this difference. The witness has just said that there were certain secondary or subsidiary buildings that were also counted. So the difference between the 30 and 40 houses and the 70 buildings she mentioned could be a result of the fact she has also referred to subsidiary buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can assist, so that I don't have to speak quietly to Ms. Nozica while interrupting her cross-examination. In the earlier transcript at page 12 between lines 12 and 14, the way the record was corrected there it says: "I think some 30 or 40 households," is the word in English, "were destroyed at the time, and that implies houses and stables." And that was the text of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that there were perhaps 70 buildings that were destroyed or damaged, and 30 or 40 of them were houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but no, that's not the case. When I stood up to put my question, I asked my colleague to find this part, the relevant part. The answer states 30 to 40 houses and stables which means that according to witness's answer -- well, she included houses and stables. Now the witness says that there were 30 houses and the auxiliary buildings were stables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll put the question to the witness. Witness, when you said that there were between 30 to 40 houses concerned, did you mean 30 to 40 houses including the stables, or when you said 30 or 40 buildings, were you just referring to houses? The stables where one keeps the animals and the houses are buildings that humans live in. So the number of 30 to 40 refers to what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 30 to 40 houses, because it's not possible for people to live in stables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, but I believe that you'll go back to page 12 of the transcript, lines 12, 13 and 14, and there you will see that the answer was quite different from the explanation now provided, but we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: As far as these two individuals are concerned, the Presiding Judge asked you about someone called Marko Livajsic. Did you know that he was an HVO commander in Uzricje? That was the question. And you said that you didn't.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. At the time I didn't know that he was a commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you know at that time, or perhaps someone told you about this later, but at any rate, up until December, 1993, did you know that he had organised the looting and torching of Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Did you know anything about Marinko Livajsic, Marinko? Did you know that he and Marko acted together and looted and torched Muslim houses? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. In response to a question put to you by my learned colleague or the Presiding Judge, you said that you had seen those two individuals in the village during the period that you were there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were they also camouflaged? Were their faces painted and you recognised them in spite of this fact, or perhaps their faces hadn't been painted.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the shelling and nine days and nights, no, I didn't see them. After the nine-day period had ended, I saw them in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question was when you saw them, were their faces painted or not?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, their faces hadn't been painted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So they did move a around the village without having painted their faces. There were some individuals whose faces hadn't been painted and they moved around the village, some soldiers. It's not necessary to say who. Or perhaps I should be more precise. Did you see any HVO members in the village whose faces hadn't been painted after this nine-day period had ended?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I only saw them on one occasion. I'm not sure of the date. That's when I saw them, though, when someone was killed in Uzricje. Two Croats were killed. And they took us out of those two houses that we were staying in. We were taken in front of the house, Omer Filipovic, and that's when I saw them there with other Croatian soldiers. I saw Marinko and Marko there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Since we're talking about the two Croats who were killed, can you remember what you were told about the location at which they were killed at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: They were killed there, because when you enter the village of Uzricje, well, there are three access routes, and when you leave the village, these three routes join and become one route, and at the end of that road, well, that's where those two Croats were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So one could draw the conclusion that they were killed just above your village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. On a number of occasions you said today that the shelling and shooting lasted for nine days in the village. It started on the 13th and went on for nine days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge, you mentioned whether you had given a statement after the war on the 13th of January, 1993. It says 1999 in the transcript. Perhaps I made a mistake. I was saying in a response put to you by the Presiding Judge, you said that you didn't give any statements after the war apart from the statement that we're discussing today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: On the 6th of March, 1994, in the course of the war, did you give a statement of any kind about these events?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you give the SDB, the State Security Service in Bugojno, rather, the security services centre in Zenica, a statement on the 6th of March, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: In Zenica, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, would that be this statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about 1994, madam. Try and remember that. Let's make this easier for everyone. I'll now ask the usher, and for the sake of the transcript, I'd like to point out that the statement concerned is dated the 6th of March, 1994. The witness allegedly gave to the State Security Service in Bugojno. The witness can confirm this. And perhaps this is an exhibit that the Prosecution provided us with. Could the usher, please, place this statement on the ELMO so that the witness can see it and so that she can verify whether the signature is her signature. I will then have a couple of questions I'd like to put to her about the statement. Could you please have a look at the bottom of the document to see whether the signature is yours. Have a look at the top of the document to see where and when this took place. Can you try and remember whether you gave this statement? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't my intention to tender this statement. I won't be doing this. I just want to point out a couple of details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, you said that you don't intend to tender this document. You're raising an issue. Well, quite rightly, but you're showing the witness a document, you're putting questions to her, and the Judges are in a disadvantageous position because we're not familiar with the contents of this statement. I will discuss the matter with my colleagues, but as a rule, when one shows the witness a document, it's almost an obligation to request that the document be admitted into evidence, because if one doesn't do this, and this could be important for you, too, if one doesn't do this and if the witness provides an answer favourable to you, but you don't have a document to support the testimony, in that case well, what is the probative value of this testimony? So you're harming yourselves. I don't know whether you have correctly understood that when you present a document and put questions to the witness on the basis of the document, it's in your interest to request that the document be admitted into evidence. This is in your favour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I accept this criticism. It's not my intention to tender this document into evidence. Could we take this off -- this document off the ELMO. I'll just put a few questions to the witness now, but I won't be tendering the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you like.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Madam, could you please tell me something about the date. Perhaps immediately after this event, did you have a different opinion with regard to the time period during which this took place? Is it possible that you said this event, the shooting in the village, took place from the 13th of January to the 18th of January, 1993? I'm asking you whether it's -- you're sure that it was a nine-day period that was involved, or did it continue up until the 18th of January, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as the shelling is concerned, it continued for nine days and nine nights. But the torching, that continued.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So you stand by your statement that it lasted for nine days. Let's move on. In your statement, you said that dugouts were dug by Muslims and Croats together?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When did this take place? When was this done?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it was done from November onwards. I think it was in the course of November and December. I think that's when they made these dugouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, can you tell me the following in response to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge about whether these constructions were concrete constructions: Well, you said that there were planks that had been used. So in fact were -- was timber used? Were logs used for these dugouts?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant, but I didn't articulate this quite clearly. I didn't know how to put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the interpretation to finish. So in order to help you, we're talking about logs cut in half and then they're put together; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is that one of the ways in which such dugouts are created in Bosnia and Herzegovina when one wants to take shelter or when one goes into the mountains? Is this the way one usually makes dugouts?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You've never had the opportunity for seeing such things?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Well, this was a necessary form of accommodation, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you whether this had been intended as accommodation, but when dugouts of that kind are made, is this how they're made?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was never in the mountains, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When you mentioned the extent of the damage and the houses that had been destroyed in the village as a result of the shelling, you said that almost all of the houses had been either destroyed or damaged. Can you tell me something about the extent of the damage? Was the damage significant? Had they been completely destroyed as a result of the shelling? I'm talking about the shelling now.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most of the houses -- most of the roofs on the houses had been hit.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we say that if the houses hadn't been destroyed, the damage inflicted on them was significant?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we could say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You mentioned two houses that you lived in. They were the property of Bosniaks. They hadn't been hit. They hadn't been destroyed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: They remained intact. Have I understood you correctly when you mentioned feeding the livestock. You said that you went out to do this on one occasion with your father-in-law, but your father-in-law continued to go out and to feed the livestock?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have I understood you correctly then?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, at the time in the village during the critical period that we're referring to, was your sister present in the village together with her family?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, my sister was in Ibrahim Kurbegovic's house. We weren't together. I was in Cazim Kurbegovic's house, and she was in Ibrahim Kurbegovic's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that you weren't together at all. You weren't in the dugout together?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were in the dugout together, but what I'm saying is that after we left the dugout, they were in one house and I was in another house.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were those houses very far from each other?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the distance between the dugouts was about 20 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you know when your sister left that house? Did you receive any such information if you didn't see that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: She left the house before we did, before we left our house.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How do you know that? Do you know how she left the house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I know that they left on foot, and I didn't know where or how she -- I don't know where she went or how she left the house until I had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But how do you know that she had left? Did someone tell you on that day that your sister had left?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: She was seen through the window because she had to pass through -- pass by that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this because a response to a question put to you by the Presiding Judge today, you said that as far as you know while you were staying in that house, none of the Bosniaks left the village and now we have established that she and her family left the village, and since that's the case, I'll ask you whether you know whether anyone from your house or from the other house left the village in a similar way?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I started to say something about that in response to that question. I don't know why I stopped, but I was saying something about whether someone had left the village or not. After that, after my sister had left, some others had left. I think they left together.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you be a little more precise? Your sister's family, her sister-in-law, her children, et cetera, is that who you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But I'm asking you whether anyone else left? If you know or not. If you don't know, it doesn't matter, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll now go back to the -- to what you said about how the Croats -- Croat women left the village. You said they were afraid of Serbian shelling. The Presiding Judge asked you whether you were afraid. You said they'd shell for a while and then you'd be able to stay on there. On the basis of your sister's experience, she had to flee from Gornji Vakuf, wouldn't you have drawn the conclusion that during that period of time, you should also leave the village because you were afraid of Serbian shelling or did someone in the village say, members of the Territorial Defence, perhaps, that you shouldn't leave the village, that the Serbs wouldn't attack the village. Why were you sure, that given the situation, given the situation in which the Croatian women were leaving and given the fact that your sister had been expelled from Donji Vakuf, given this experience, why did you believe you could shelter in the village and that everything would pass?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. At that time you weren't -- you didn't feel safe and you didn't feel threatened either. I don't know myself why we didn't leave. Everyone regretted the fact later. Where should we have gone? If we had gone to Gornji Vakuf -- from Uzricje to Gornji Vakuf, well, that's what we had in mind because we were allies with the Croats at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: But, madam, Croatian women were leaving the village regardless of the fact that they were allies. But you were told or you had indicia according to which this village might be attacked. I would like to know whether you and your husband discussed the matter, and then you decided that all Muslims or Bosniaks should leave or did some Muslims leave with the Croats, some Muslim women?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim women didn't leave at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I've heard that 10 times now. I'm asking you whether your men decided about this. Did they discuss the matter? Did you women discuss the matter? How did this happen? Did you see your husband, or did you see your husband or did you discuss the matter? Did you know about some agreement according to which everyone should remain together in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was an agreement of any kind. We just stayed on. I'm telling you, I don't know what the reason was, but we stayed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you're not answering the question that Ms. Nozica is putting to you. It's a very interesting question. She's -- she's asking you whether you discussed the matter with your husband, and you say, "Well, we stayed on." Did you discuss the matter with your husband, and did you tell yourselves, well, certain women have left, should I also leave in order to be safe? That's the purpose of the question. So what would you say? Did you discuss the matter or not? Try and answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course, there was talk about this, but where to? Where? How?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica has touched upon another subject in her question, and that is whether your husband and you had any indication that an attack was possible, that it was imminent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. How could I have any indication? I ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Madam Nozica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, though you're a witness, you're asking where should the Muslim families go. When there are disasters and when people have to leave their residences, this is a normal question. But my question to you is: Did you have any idea where the Croatian women could go? Because if the Muslim women didn't know where to go, in your opinion, where could the Croatian women go according to your knowledge? What possibilities did they have in the village or in the surroundings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They went to Mackovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there a Croat -- a Croatian community there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, only Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was there a village or a hamlet, for instance, the Mahala that was inhabited only by Muslims, that wasn't far from you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was in town in Gornji Vakuf. This is a street called Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How far is that from your village and was it mostly inhabited by Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: About two and a half kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And my second question, I am repeating, was it inhabited mostly by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge that during the conflicts some of the Bosniaks went to Croatia? Did you have any knowledge of that? Do you know today of any people having left in that direction?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: You meanwhile we were at Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: No, I'm talking during the war, during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You never heard that someone went to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I heard afterwards, towards the end of 1993, but at the time I really didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I asked you for the whole period. I wasn't thinking just of January, 1993, please. I think this is rather important. In answer to a question from His Honour, whether you had any indication that something would happen, some attack, you said no, but didn't you say a moment ago, that you were told that the Serbs would attack? Didn't you say that, "My sister was expelled from Donji Vakuf together with some other refugees because of the Serbs"? Wasn't that an indication that something could happen? Wasn't this an indication for you to --

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: But, madam, I really didn't know what could happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, that is a different answer.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have to ask you some questions about Jusuf Softic and Plivcic Tahir, and you said today that you saw them being led by HVO soldiers to Jusuf Softic's house, in that direction. Is that all you saw?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: How did you know where and how they were killed? Who told you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I said that too. When we -- our names were being taken down in Ibro's house, Ibro came and told us that they had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did he tell you that a sniper rifle had been found in Jusuf Softic's house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, he said nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: The men who were in the village, who you said were defending the village, did they have weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Some Kalashnikovs and some hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did anyone ask them to surrender those weapons when you left the dugouts?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did any HVO soldier ask whether anyone in the village had sniper rifles, whether there were snipers in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I really have no knowledge of weapons. I don't know whether there were any. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was whether any HVO soldier had asked whether there were snipers in the village, whether they were being concealed when the TO soldiers surrendered the other weapons. I'm asking you this because you said that in your statement. It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did ask who had weapons. "Does anyone have a sniper?"

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, please, where were the men from your village? What were their positions? Where were they operating against the Croats, if at all, and do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know because I -- I didn't see them, how far away they were. I really can't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did they fight against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think in order to protect us, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a little surprised by your answer. Everyone was living in a village. All the people knew the links among the villagers, and in such a situation, when villagers are ensuring the security of the village with weapons if necessary, and you tell us, "I don't know. I'm not aware of this." Is that really the truth that you're telling us, that you were totally unaware where the villagers who were protecting your village were situated? Your neighbours or maybe your husband. I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it is true that I don't know, because I was in the dugout. So I really don't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before taking shelter, the men of the village, they were around the village from time to time. If they were to ensure the protection of the village, you must have known where they were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The men were there. Now, what you're saying, whether they were digging or providing a shelter for themselves, they may have done that during the nine nights, but I really do not know, and I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I followed with interest the last half an hour the questioning mainly about the reasons why the witness stayed at home and she didn't flee. This I understand, that it should have been clarified, but somehow I feel also now that the -- the questions put during the last couple of minutes also might have -- might have indicated that even the witness is now an accused if she stayed there in her village. She very clearly stated before that they didn't have anyplace to go and how to go there, and it was the first question and first answer. Now, the other issue is where the men happened to be during that time. We all know that there were persons who were able-bodied persons with weapons, they left in those circumstances and either they joined one or the other group. It was true for the Croats. It was true for the Bosniaks. And that is why for me the very purpose of listening to this witness is what happened in that village, in Uzricje, and it is what I would like to hear from the witness. And I finish now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, but I will be very brief. I don't intend to elaborate on the reasons for my questions, but the same reason is for the question why the Muslims said, as the Prosecutor insisted on the question why the Croats left. The implication is that the Croats knew of the attack. So the same reason may apply to the Bosniaks, because if somebody in the village tells you there will be an attack by the Serbs and then a part of the inhabitants leaves and the other part doesn't leave, then after all is indicative. I didn't insist only on the question why the witness didn't leave, but through the witness, I wanted to establish why the other Bosniaks also didn't leave, and I'm trying to establish the reason for such a decision. Each one of us had to make such a decision at some point of time, but I think this is extremely important because of the questions put by the Prosecutor about this topic. Thank you. I will be very brief and end my questioning soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that when you left the dugouts and when you went to the Mahala, and on page 49, lines 4 and 5, you said that you left with your children. Where did your husband go?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We all went to the Mahala in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was your husband with you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did your husband join the forces of the BH army or the TO when you went to Mahala?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Normally he did. Whether it was the army or the TO, he did join, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: When was this, madam?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't tell you exactly what month it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: While your husband was in the village, did he have any role in organising the reception of the women, the defence of the village, or in any such way, or do you know of any other Muslim who was perhaps the most important among equals?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We had this Zahid Hozic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What was he?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He was -- I don't know how they called him, whether he was president of the local commune or something like that. Anyway, he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Was he also among the armed Bosniaks in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That is my question. I'm asking you among the armed Bosniaks, who was the leader, the commander, whatever you like to call him? Do you know that, and whether it was your husband?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't my husband.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And do you know whether there was any such person, and do you know him by name?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Finally, did you ever talk to your husband when you set off from the village. Did you ever talk to him about the positions of the Muslims or Bosniaks in the village? Where were they? Weren't you worried when you didn't know where they were during the shelling? Did you talk about this?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, the most important thing for us was to see one another.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. I'm asking you something else. Did you ask him, "Where were you?"

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Of course we did talk about this. But you never got an answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I see. He didn't give you an answer. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You never get a real answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have to make a break now. So we're going to resume at 10 to 1.00, and we will have almost an hour left, as there are three Defence counsels left, but we need to end at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifteen minutes you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave and in agreement with the other Defence counsel, only my learned friend Alaburic and myself will have some questions, so we'll share the time left to us more or less equally, and we will certainly finish before the end, and Mr. Praljak is telling me that he may have five minutes of questions himself, and we'll count that in. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Madam Witness. I won't use your name even though you're not under protective measures. This discussion that we were having with my learned friend Madam Nozica when she asked you whether your husband ever told you where he and the other men were in those days, you said that you never really got an answer from him. My question is why you didn't get an answer?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you think that perhaps this may have been a military secret that he didn't want to reveal?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so, because I don't think you tell your wife everything either. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you knew that your husband was active in the military?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: He was in defence of the village, and then when we got there, he joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he was among those who had weapons, and in fact, your husband had a Kalashnikov issued to him.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the help of the usher, can I put a document on the ELMO, please. I will have a few questions for you, and I may be showing you another document. On the basis of a document that I have in my hand, it is an HVO document of the security and information service, and the centre of that service, dated the 18th of March, 1997. This is a note made in 1997. That is a couple of years after the events. And this HVO service was aware of what was happening in Uzricje, obviously. And on the basis of this statement, I would like to ask you a few questions to see how much you know about these events. Do you know a man called Enver Sljivo from the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that such a man lived in the village of Dusa and would come to the village of Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I do know that he lived in Dusa, but I do not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Croat men had surrendered their weapons to the Muslim soldiers before these events?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Croat soldiers in the village before this attack that we discussed on the 13th of January, that the Croatian soldiers had handed over their weapons to Muslim men -- or, rather, to the Territorial Defence in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you hadn't heard anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before the 13th of January there were certain discussions between the Croats and the Muslims in the village, that is, between the TO and the village HVO? There was a discussion about the surrender of weapons and what would happen.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear anything about this even after the war?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, because I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person in the village by the name of Smajo Hozic?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you also know Zahid Hozic? You mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they have any positions in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that Zahid was president of the local commune. Now, what we -- he was in that particular area, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some of the Croats in the village, specifically Mijo Ivankovic and Mato Ivankovic and Mira Livajsic were sleeping just before the 13th in Abida Hozic's house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How far was Abida's Hozic's house from your house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We were in the centre of the village and they were at the top of the village, towards the end of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I won't ask you any more questions about that. Thank you. You're claiming that you don't know anything about the relationship between the TO and the HVO in the village before this attack. That is your statement.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, madam, please, you described the houses that the Croats put you up in after you left the dugout. Is it true that a group of Muslims was put in Seketa Sukrija's house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: A woman stayed behind there. She was bedridden. Her name was Zlata Seketa, because for years, for years she was immobile, and they left her daughter-in-law to take care of her there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in this third house there was this bedridden woman and her son-in-law and no one else?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but also her son.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And no one else apart from that family?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Regarding the dugouts, before you were taken to those houses, you said that there were about 400 inhabitants in the village just before the attack; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Three hundred to 400. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't count them. That is just an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how many out of that number, again, your estimate, were locals and how many were refugees? Roughly.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were perhaps some 20 or so refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you also told us that those refugees had come from Donji Vakuf and Modrica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there any from other locations?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let us say that there was -- there were 300 people and two dugouts, and you described the size of those dugouts. Then there would be about 150 in each of those dugouts. That is physically not possible. Is it true that some people had already left before that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The people in the lower dugout, they left. How they left and when they left, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that they left before they got into the dugout?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know how to explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe it's my mistake. Let us take it slowly. The moment you decided to go into the dugout, there were, according to what you said, about 300 to 400 Muslims in the village. Let us say there were 300. The smaller figure. It half went to one dugout and the other half to the other, it would mean that there were about 150 in an area that was about 4 by 4 that you said. That is physically not possible. Now, my question is: The group in the dugout that you were in, is it possible that there were 150 people there?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know the exact figure, but we were packed full. It was very tight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My next question in that connection. Are you sure that all those Muslims that you mentioned that were in the village when the conflict started, are you sure that a part of those people had not fled the village before the conflict or just -- or during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: A part of them did escape during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that means that some people, during the conflict, at some point in time during the conflict, fled the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And then another part, another number, stayed in the village.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you don't know how many of you were in the dugout when you were there?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I could name them, the people, but that would take us two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, can we come to some sort of an agreement? Give us a rough estimate, although you said you were there for about three weeks [as interpreted]. Were there 20 or more than 20?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: More than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were there 40?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Something like that. Forty or 50. I don't -- something like that. I'm afraid of making a mistake. I just know that there were quite a lot of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Have you any idea how many people were in the first dugout?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. We heard from the previous witness that it was not possible to leave the dugout while you were in it, but today you told us that it was possible to leave, at least during the night.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I did leave, so I can say that as regards myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you don't know what the situation was in the other dugout?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would there be any reason for things to be different over there?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, if you can remember, when I intervened when you used the word "people distributed themselves," and then you told us, and this is page 33, line 9, you said that Croats and Muslims did distribute themselves before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, I submit to you that when the conflict started, the Croats left the positions that they had taken up. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you will allow that the Muslims and the Croats stayed in the positions that they had taken up?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, but what happened later, I don't know. I really don't know, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. So you don't know. You told us a little about the way decisions were made in the village, would you stay or would you leave. My learned friend asked you about that. I would like to get some other information from you. Madam, in that period, the end of 1992 when the first incidents occurred in Donji Vakuf and then the beginning of 1993, January, when a larger-scale conflict occurred, did you have any occasion to see the state authorities working or not? The usual signs. Would you see a policeman walk through the village during the day?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you receive tax forms, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean to -- bills?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, any kind of bills that you would need to pay?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we did get electricity bills, telephone bills.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So at the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, you would receive electricity bills or the rent?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. Up until November, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. So we can agree that after November, those bills no longer came.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And we can also agree that schools were not working?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: My children didn't go to school, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you give me any example before the outbreak of the conflict at the end of 1992, beginning of 1993, that there was any role of the state that was in operation?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I was a housewife, and I didn't go into town, so I don't know what was going on. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was the Territorial Defence giving the population any kind of instructions how to behave in the case of danger or even shelling?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did the BH army give you any instructions?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you're saying that in fact the people themselves, the citizens, the villagers, would reach official or unofficial agreements as to how the people in the village would behave?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So these were decisions taken on the spot by the citizens; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's what -- you could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On page 36, line 13, you said that you were in the dugouts, and then you said that they, the men who had rifles, were a little above the dugouts. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you know that they were at some position when you say they were above the dugout.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they have trenches of any kind? Did they have a stronghold?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But then how do you know that they were above?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they weren't there in the dugout. The dugout was in the hill, in the little hill, and they were around the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Perhaps they were at the foot of the hill.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. That's why I'm saying -- well, perhaps I said that they were above quite by chance. I don't know whether they had dug themselves in. I don't know whether they did any digging in the course of the night. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that on two occasions you said I -- you couldn't remember exactly, but you made an assessment and said that you remained in Uzricje, in Kurbegovic's house, up until around March or April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The statement referred to by my colleague Senka Nozica, I'd like to refer to that statement, and I'd like to say that you were in Bugojno on the 6th of March. Could we agree that at the beginning of the March you were in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, I wasn't sure. I don't know whether we were there up until March or April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And do you remember having been asked by the State Security Service in Bugojno to give a statement and you gave a brief statement?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. In March 1994.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Because that was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And I have another minor matter. You've described how people lived in the village, but perhaps we should explain how people lived traditionally in the houses, in the villages over there. Did you use fire or electricity for your heating?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: We used -- we used wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So every autumn would the people prepare the necessary firewood for the heating?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And in Kurbegovic's house that you stayed in, had they prepared firewood?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was the case in other surrounding houses?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there was a firewood stove in the house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you used that stove?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was in the kitchen?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But there were stoves in other rooms and you used firewood there?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So there were several stoves?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me if I say you weren't cold in the house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't cold.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as the electricity is concerned, could we agree that the entire village didn't have electricity?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was the case as of October or November, 1992? Is that the case, that there was no electricity then?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that the electricity supply was cut that night when the shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And before that date the electricity supply was cut only occasionally?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. As far as the food is concerned, preparing oneself for winter, would it be true to say that in your village as in the surrounding villages in autumn, the late autumn, the villagers would provisions home to survive for the winter? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was it customary for people to stock up on potatoes for the winter?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: They also had cured meat?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: They also had freezers where they freeze meat and vegetables for the winter?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's also correct, but they couldn't be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And finally, while you were in Kurbegovic's house, you weren't hungry, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, we weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Another two or three questions. We saw the video that was shown, and you identified certain things. On two occasions you identified a certain individual, and you identified the place where basketball was played at the end of the village. As far as that is concerned, do you know who made the video?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone using cameras to film things in the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And we saw some scenes depicting soldiers' positions, or we saw them from behind or in semi-profile. I never noticed any insignia. Could you perhaps say something about those soldiers? Do you know which army they were a member of?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to say whether they were members of the armija or the TO?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you couldn't say that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also saw some places that one would call positions, in military terms. Did you recognise any of those positions in Uzricje, that might be in Uzricje?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see them very well, but I couldn't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Praljak, you have five minutes now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you said that in November there was some shooting in Vakuf. That was after the conflict in Prozor on the 26th of July -- on the 26th or 7th of October. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was in Prozor, but in November, I know there was shooting in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said that the HVO launched an attack. Did you then leave the village and see who had attacked whom?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At a distance of two kilometres you heard shooting for several hours and nothing else; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We had a look at a video, and I saw five or six houses that had been torched. Did you see more than that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: As I have said, I didn't see things very clearly in the video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I saw 120-millimetre mortar. Do you know who that mortar belonged to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I saw a 12.7 machine-gun which was being used. Do you know who owned the machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I saw a well-prepared trench. They must have spent a long time digging it. Do you know who was in the trench and to whom the trench belonged?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. You said the shooting lasted for nine days, and Judge Antonetti asked you about that. If every five minutes over a 12-day period you fire one shell, that amounts to 648 shells. Would those calculations be correct? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you this: Yes, I was under the impression that it was every five minutes. Whether that assessment of mine is correct or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Madam, I was involved in the war, and I believe you. You are under that impression. That really was the case. You were very afraid. You were in great danger. One is in great danger, and that is why one has certain impressions, and I thank you for saying that you were under that impression. That is a good and frank answer, but my question is as follows: Did you sleep in the dugouts?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You remained standing for nine days in the dugouts?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't remain standing. We would sit down back to back.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: If people sit down in an area of 12 square metres, well, it's very easy to calculate that not even 30 people can sit down in an area of 12 metres, 12 square metres.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said there were women, children, elderly people. The younger people were not in the dugout.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. In the video that we'll probably use later on, there are certain panorama shots that show that a lot of houses and roofs hadn't been damaged at the time of -- at the time the video was made. Did you see that too?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you also notice that some of the houses that had been torched didn't show signs of having been hit by shells? You could only see that they had been burnt with the exception of two that were destroyed. But again, we don't know what was the cause of this destruction.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, not necessarily. That's not necessarily the case. It depends on the angle the video was made from. It wasn't just the roof. Perhaps the wall had been damaged too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You said you weren't an arms expert. We had an English professional here and he said that when a mortar shell falls 40 metres from the target, then you could say that the hit is good. You're not a military expert, but could you assume that impossible to use a weapon of any kind to hit certain houses or certain targets from a certain distance? My question is as follows: You spent nine days in this dugout. How far was the dugout from the house you were accommodated in? What was the distance between the dugout and the house?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was up to 150 to 200 metres -- up to 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And during that period time, you'd go to that house with HVO soldiers. Did you ever walk around the village and count the houses? If there are 40 houses that are destroyed, it's necessary to count them, or would you also say that you were under the impression that that was the number of houses that had been damaged? Did you ever count them?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And later when on one occasion you left the house to go to the stable, which was in the vicinity of the house, on that occasion, you weren't able to count the houses and you didn't do that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I never counted them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: There's just one document that I'd like now to show you. Could we please place it on the ELMO and I will later tender the document. Please have a look at it. But in the meantime I'll put my question to you. In my opinion you're quite right to fear revenge being taken. I regret the fact that you weren't granted protective measures. You live in a divided society, and in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, people still take revenge today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And you don't have any faith in the legal system in place in that state; is that correct? You don't believe that the state will protect, that they will protect your daughters from someone who might want to harm them, you don't believe that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I ought to believe that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Well, there are many things one ought to do, but I want to know whether you have faith in them or whether you are afraid? I would be afraid.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm also afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the course of the war, was the possibility of someone taking revenge even greater given that that there were individuals who had been involved in disputes, who had feuds that had been going on for 10 years. Were there such acts of revenge?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So would you have felt safer in the houses with HVO soldiers or would you have felt safer if these HVO soldiers hadn't been in front of the houses? At that point in time, were you safer with those soldiers in front houses or would you have been safer if they hadn't been there?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer that question. I don't know. I would have been afraid in both situations.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Please have a look at this document and could you please read out the first sentence. Could we have it on the ELMO. Please read out the first sentence. It says -- the sentence under sector IPD?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: "The list of wounded."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: "The list of HVO members who were wounded and killed in the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH in Gornji Vakuf from the 12th of January to the 24th of February, 1993."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you have a look at the last page, please. Could the usher show you the last page. And can you read out what it says up until "total". It says "wounded killed, soldiers wounded".

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: "Wounded soldiers, 209. Killed 46. Wounded civilians 7. Civilians killed 14. Total 276."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. I would like to tender this document into evidence through this witness if the Court allows me to do so. If not, I'll tender it into evidence on some other occasion. Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. While waiting, I'll have a look at the document. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a few questions. We have about another 12 minutes until the end of this hearing. I think it would be important for us and particularly for the Judges to see whether your village, the village of Uzricje, is on an important road. From the direction of Pidris, was it possible to pass through Uzricje in order to reach Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If the Prozor-Gornji Vakuf main road was blocked, whatever the reason, could someone come from Pidris via Uzricje to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the main road.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So far we have seen numerous documents and UNPROFOR documents as well. One was dated the 11th of January, and in that document it says that there is information according to which the Muslims had shut down Gornji Vakuf and had set up check-points. Were you aware of the fact that the Muslim forces had done that on the 11th of January?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. I wasn't in town at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the OTP, you said that the Muslims mostly lived in the central and lower part of the village, whereas the Croats lived in the upper part of the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that two dugouts had been constructed, one in the lower part of the village and another in the central part of the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That means that in the Croatian part of the village not a single dugout had been made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I said in the upper part, I said that because in the lower part, where the Muslims were, there were two or three Croatian houses, and similarly, in the upper part, most of the houses were Muslim, but in the upper part, the houses were exclusively Croat houses. I don't know whether there was a dugout up there in the upper part, but I know about these two dugouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So does that mean you that you are no longer claiming with such certainty that only two dugouts had been made?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm only aware of the existence of two dugouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. So that means that you are not aware of the fact that in the upper part of the town inhabited by Croats there was a dugout?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You also said that members of the Territorial Defence or the ABiH - it doesn't matter what we call them - were mainly in an area about 50 metres from the dugout either above or below the dugout; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That means that your army's positions were in the central and lower part of the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said that not a single Croatian house in Uzricje had been damaged as a result of the shelling, which is why I'll ask you the following: Was it mostly the central and lower part of the village that were shelled? That's where you were located, and that's where the positions of your army members were.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the upper central part, which was an exclusively Muslim part, was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what about the lower part of the village where the second dugout was located and where members of your army were? Was that part of the village also shelled?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: No. Those houses had only been torched.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You said the houses were torched. Was that when you left the dugout or after -- after that?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: When we left the dugout. Well, I mean on that day and later on?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you left, the houses in the lower part of the village had been torched. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had been torched on that day exactly. But as of that day, they continued with the torch in question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you left the dugout, had they already been torched?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in our part.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the lower part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When did you see the houses in the lower part of the village?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the torched ones?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Of any kind. Not torched houses. When did you see houses that hadn't been torched?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the lower part, well, when we went down to the house that we were put up in.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So that means when you left the dugout, those houses hadn't been damaged. They hadn't been torched.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Not in the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That means that when you were leaving the dugout, there were Muslim houses in the village that hadn't been damaged?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That means that you didn't tell us the truth when you said that all the Muslim houses had been damaged or destroyed as a result of the shelling?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, I only wanted to say -- perhaps, I'm not that articulate. Perhaps I'm not expressing myself very well. I meant that on that day when the shelling started and -- and up until the time that I left the village, that's what I had in mind. That's when I said that they hadn't remained intact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, it's very important for us to establish which houses had been damaged or destroyed as a result of the shelling and which ones had been destroyed or damaged later on. That's the purpose of my question. Perhaps you could clarify that for us.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: The houses that were destroyed as a result of the shelling were in the central part of the village, and houses were torched in this lower part, because between those -- because there were Croatian houses among those houses, and on that occasion, only Muslim houses had been torched.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll move on. We'll leave the subject of houses, because we won't be able to clear this up right now. You told us that an HVO soldier who called himself Pile allowed you to leave the house on a daily basis to feed the livestock, but he asked you to return by 4.00 in the afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that all of you could leave the house and feed the livestock or carry out other tasks outside?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If this HVO soldier asked you to return by 4.00 in the afternoon, it would be logical to draw the conclusion that he wasn't on guard while you were guarding or feeding the livestock or doing other things outside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What sort of livestock are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, cows, sheep, chickens, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you had been hungry, could you have used some of the animals that you had as food?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In January, in our area, it's quite dark. Night falls quite early; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At 4.00 in the afternoon, was it already night or at least dusk?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did any of you try to flee at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
