utterances.text: Well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you all returned to the house on a voluntary basis by 4.00 p.m. as you were asked to do by the HVO member?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, could you clarify something else for us with regard to when you left the dugout. In the statement given to the Prosecution, you said, and I'll quote, it's on page 7 of the B/C/S version, and I quote: "A day before we were arrested, our men concluded that they couldn't hold the village and that it was very dangerous to linger there. They said we should all flee to the Muslim part of Gornji Vakuf. First some men left, and they were followed by women, children, and the elderly who had taken shelter in the dugout in the lower part of the village. The remaining men stayed with the women and children who hid in the dugouts in the central part of the village. Once the people had left the dugout in the lower part of the village, this area was taken over by HVO soldiers, and they shut down the corridor in the direction of Gornji Vakuf, which meant that we, who were hiding in the dugout in the central part of the village, and that included the men who had remained with us, were in a trap." So does that mean that other inhabitants from the other dugouts informed you of their intention to leave and to go to Gornji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what they informed us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say, "Our men decided that they could no longer hold the village," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, these people who were with us in the dugout.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That means members of your army who were with you. Those are "our men."

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, our people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have "our men" in mind or all the people who were in the dugout including women?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, those people who were in the dugout. My husband and my father, my father-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So men on the whole.

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And now I'll probably only have enough time for this question that concerns your departure from the village. Today, you said on page 11, in the second part of page 11, you said that in March or April, you're not sure exactly when, a truce was agreed, and you then started cleaning up your homes. You also said that your husband and children also went to clean up your house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that up until that point in time -- or at that time, it was possible for you to leave the house freely? No one had to authorise you to leave? No one asked you to return by some point in time?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How long did this period during which you were free to move around last? During which you were free to leave the house you were in?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't answer that with any precision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's not necessary to be precise, but could you say whether that lasted for two or three days or perhaps a little longer?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, something like that. And we rejoiced since everything was over. Everyone could go to their home.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What sort of condition was your house in when you went to clean it up?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was completely burnt down and it didn't have a roof. It had been -- the walls had been damaged by the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At that time, no one prevented you from going to see whomever you wanted to see. You were quite free to move around; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIJADA KURBEGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to stop. We have to stop now because there's a hearing after us, and we cannot exceed our time. Very quickly now, concerning the admission of documents. Mr. Mundis, what do you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution tenders the videotape P 1027 and document P 7350. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the Defence. Mr. Praljak has asked to tender the document with the list of killed and wounded from the HVO. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender the document I put on the ELMO. It will have a number tomorrow. It is the minutes from the 18th of March, 1997, from the SIS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, one very short point in light of Your Honour's declining to grant protective measures, we submit the consequential upon that, that that part of the transcript from this morning, which we submit was effectively provisionally in closed session pending that decision should form part of the public transcript. I'm not referring to the other passage relating to health. That can stay where it is, Your Honour, but the passage relating to protective measures we submit should now be public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will rule on those requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... object to the admission of document P 7350 for the same reasons as I outlined yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is time to adjourn. Madam, the Chamber thanks you for coming to testify in The Hague. We wish you all the best and a safe journey home. We will all resume work here tomorrow at 9.00 a.m. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 27th day of October, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
